headline: Out of Oleshky. Their daughters were waiting.
summary: Evacuees from Russian-held Oleshky crossed into Ukraine on Saturday, by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. A ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump got them out; it runs through Sunday. Relatives waited at the border with aid tents and pet food. Liza Paliy, 19, last saw her father 2½ years ago. Ukraine won't say how many came.

cover_question.q: Why couldn't they just walk home?

cover_answer: The short road was mined. They went the long way round.
table_question: Would you work with someone you hate to get people home?

5-7.script: Some families in Ukraine got their dads back today. They had been stuck in a city called Oleshky, and the short road out had land mines, so buses took them the long way round through two other countries. Think of your longest car trip; this one was longer. At the end, daughters waited at the border, and the grown-ups had food ready.
5-7.why: One long trip home, one person waiting at the end. That is the whole story at six.
5-7.why_long: A child this age reasons from what is in front of them, so the script hands them one picture: a long bus trip home, and a daughter at the border. The war, the occupation and the ombudsman are not in it. Expect "did everyone get out?" Several hundred chose to stay, and food is being brought in to them.

8-12.script: Russia took Oleshky early in the war, and the roads out were mined, so about 2,000 people were stuck with little food. This week both sides paused the shooting there, like a timeout in a game, and the road got cleared. Buses took people out through Russia and Belarus, and on Saturday they crossed home.
8-12.why: Stuck, pause, road cleared, buses, home. Five links they can follow in order.
8-12.why_long: This age is building chains of cause and effect, so the script runs one: the road was mined, so people were stuck; both sides paused the shooting; the road was cleared; buses got out. The timeout is the mechanism they know. Expect "will the shooting start again Sunday?" Nobody has said it won't. The pause was for this.

13-17.script: Would you shake hands with the enemy to get people out? Ukraine's human rights chief rode into Oleshky beside his Russian counterpart to run this, and some Ukrainians hated the sight. Second: Ukraine won't say how many came home, to protect those who stayed. Is secrecy part of a rescue?
13-17.why: Working with the occupier got people out and sickened some. Let them weigh it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: standing beside the occupier's envoy got people out, and some Ukrainians could not stomach the sight. Argument is a practised skill, Kuhn says, so let them argue the ombudsman's side and then the critics'. Expect "would you have done it?" Answer honestly, and say what it would cost you.

5-7.q: Why couldn't they just walk home?
5-7.a: The short road had land mines. So the buses went the long way round, and got there safe.

8-12.q: Why go through Russia to get to Ukraine?
8-12.a: The bridges are gone and the riverbank is mined. The safe road ran long.
Both sides, in a pause Melania Trump brokered. It runs through Sunday.

13-17.q: Would you deal with the enemy to get people out?
13-17.a: Ukraine's ombudsman did, to save lives, he said. Some recoiled.

13-17.q: Why won't Ukraine say how many came home?
13-17.a: To protect those who stayed and the next mission, organizers say.
